findings.title: Offset delivery differs by route
findings.text: Earth Search applied the offset during COG conversion for some items and exposes per-asset scale and offset that describe the remaining conversion. The Copernicus Data Space exposes per-asset scale and offset in the catalog. Earth Engine pre-applies a shift back to the older range. Sentinel Hub harmonizes by default and clamps negative reflectance to zero. Planetary Computer and the requester-pays buckets document nothing. The store records conversion state per asset.

findings.title: Reader defaults disagree on scale and offset
findings.text: rioxarray leaves values unscaled by default. xarray.open_zarr scales by default. stackstac applies catalog scale and offset by default. odc-stac ignores them. A workflow that mixes these tools can apply the offset zero, one, or two times.

findings.title: One workflow resamples every band by default
findings.text: stackstac upscales every band to the finest asset resolution with nearest neighbour unless told otherwise. odc-stac returns one requested resolution. rasterio keeps native resolution unless asked for another array size. Sentinel Hub and Earth Engine resample on the provider side by default. Practice P3 holds only where the default is overridden.

findings.title: No library default selects pixels for a 10 m pond
findings.text: GDAL rasterization uses pixel centres unless ALL_TOUCHED is set. openEO polygon aggregation counts pixels whose centre is inside. A 10 m pond can select zero pixels under either default. exactextract offers a per-pixel coverage fraction instead. The selection rule is assumption A20.

findings.title: Some workflows lose tile provenance
findings.text: odc-stac fuses overlapping items by first valid pixel. Sentinel Hub stitches tiles and hides the tile grid. stackstac needs one shared projection. Windowed reads keep the native geotransform. Adjacent tiles differ in their overlap, claim G11 in the best-practices document, so a workflow that hides the tile cannot record which value it stored.

findings.title: Read cost follows blocks touched, not water bodies
findings.text: A windowed read moves only the bytes a window needs. GDAL's partial download default is 16 KB and its COG creation default is 512 pixel tiles. A lazy stack defaults to 1024 pixel chunks. A datacube reads whole chunks. A full-tile fetch moves a 110 km tile. These are tool defaults, not measured properties of delivered assets. They are the reasoning behind assumption A17, which stays unmeasured.

findings.title: Quality layers differ by route
findings.text: Sampled catalog items show different quality assets: cloud and snow probability on a Collection 1 COG item, and classification, aerosol, and water vapour on an older-collection item pointing into the Sinergise bucket. Planetary Computer documents classification, aerosol, and water vapour. Earth Engine adds Cloud Score+. Sentinel Hub adds 160 m cloud layers. HLS delivers Fmask. No documented list names the detector footprint mask that practice P11 requires. Bucket contents and availability by collection are unverified.

findings.title: Collection 1 availability is documented on two routes
findings.text: Earth Search carries Collection 1 as a separate collection whose README, as of April 2024, named gaps. The Copernicus Data Space is moving its archive to baseline 5.0 and has removed the originals, claim R2 in the best-practices document. The other routes do not document reprocessed products. Current completeness is unverified on every route.

findings.title: The 2017 history is not equally available
findings.text: Earth Search's sentinel-2-l2a collection is global from December 2018. Its Collection 1 collection had gaps as of April 2024, and a June 2022 sample is still empty. The requester-pays buckets are global from January 2017. Earth Engine starts 2017-03-28 with incomplete 2017 to 2018 coverage. Planetary Computer states 2016 onward. Sentinel Hub states January 2017. The Copernicus Data Space catalog extent starts in 2015. Assumption A10's 2017 scenario needs a route check before selection.

findings.title: Payer, region, and price differ by route
findings.text: Earth Search is provider-paid in us-west-2 with no authentication. The Sinergise buckets sit in eu-central-1, with Level-1C requester-pays and conflicting pages on Level-2A, at 0.0043 USD per 10,000 GET requests and 0.02 USD per GB to Oregon. The Copernicus Data Space is free inside quotas. Planetary Computer needs tokens and limits egress outside West Europe. Earth Engine is a subscription. Sentinel Hub is a subscription with no documented price.

findings.title: Raw pixels are reachable on every route, by different means
findings.text: Object stores return files. Sentinel Hub returns exact source values only in DN units, and its default sample type is an 8-bit stretch. Earth Engine returns arrays through batch export or a bounded synchronous call. Statistical and aggregation endpoints return one value per geometry, which fails assumption A1.

findings.title: No compute platform documents native deduplication
findings.text: Every platform documents retry. Lambda tells the function to handle duplicate events. Kubernetes may start the same program twice. Batch retries one to ten times. Spark retries a task four times. Dask retries zero times by default. Duplicate-safe writes are application work on every platform.

findings.title: Fan-out without an orchestrator exists on every platform
findings.text: Provider SNS topics announce new items. S3 event notifications invoke functions on buckets we own. Batch array jobs spawn up to 10,000 children on native queues. EMR Serverless accepts job submissions. The Dask operator runs jobs beside a cluster. Provider batch services run asynchronously. Assumption A12 does not force a scheduler onto the design.

findings.title: Function limits favour windowed reads over whole tiles
findings.text: One Lambda invocation runs at most 15 minutes with 10,240 MB. Those are ceilings, not measured runtimes. A windowed unit of work is a plausible fit. Decoding an 800 MB product, claim R4 in the best-practices document, is a resource concern that points toward containers. Neither is established until measured.

findings.title: Atomic commits and time travel come from the format or from application code
findings.text: S3 has no atomic update across keys. Iceberg and Icechunk commit atomically and serve time travel from snapshots. Plain Parquet and a chip archive get those semantics only from application code. Snapshot expiry removes time travel to expired snapshots but keeps files that surviving snapshots reference. Logical observation revisions stored as rows survive expiry. The retention policy is a separate choice.

findings.title: Small objects carry minimum charges
findings.text: Infrequent-access and Glacier Instant classes bill at least 128 KB per object and 30 or 90 days minimum. S3 Tables bills monitored objects per month. The Glue catalog bills metadata objects above a free million. Whether a chip or a partition creates such an object depends on the layout and catalog integration. These are cost inputs, not a partition rule.

findings.title: Fixed fees and quotas separate the compute platforms
findings.text: A Kubernetes cluster costs 0.10 USD per hour whether or not work is queued. Batch adds no fee over Fargate or EC2. Lambda bills per GB-second and per request. The free Copernicus tier allows two concurrent batch jobs. Earth Engine starts at 500 USD per month.

findings.title: HLS fails the size floor
findings.text: HLS is a 30 m product with two to three day latency. Assumption A7 sets a 10 m floor. HLS is documented for completeness and is not a candidate for the store.

findings.title: Latency is documented loosely
findings.text: The AWS routes state availability within a few hours of Copernicus. The Copernicus Data Space item sampled states a 24 hour timeliness. HLS states two to three days. Earth Engine, Planetary Computer, and Sentinel Hub document no latency. Assumption A11 sets no target, so this is a measurement item.

findings.title: Provider-side defaults change values silently
findings.text: Sentinel Hub's default harmonization clamps negative reflectance to zero, which is irreversible for dark water. Earth Engine's QA60 cloud mask is discontinuous from 2022 to 2024. Sentinel Hub's CLP and CLM layers are 160 m. Each default must be pinned per request before a value is stored.

findings.title: Both Earth Search collections are Element 84 conversions of the same ESA product, and why both persist is undocumented
findings.text: The registry names Element 84 as managing the GeoTIFF dataset, which holds two buckets: sentinel-cogs for the older collection and e84-earth-search-sentinel-data for Collection 1. Both are conversions of the JPEG 2000 files of the Sentinel-2 dataset, whose registry entry Element 84 also manages and whose readme Sinergise wrote. No page names the JPEG 2000 bucket's owner. Collection 1 admits baseline 05.00 and later and is documented as intended to replace the older collection, with no date. Probe PR-08 and the saved survey listings show the same product catalogued in both for recent dates. Why Collection 1 lacks most of January to November 2022 while the older collection covers it is not documented. The survey supports an inference of an incomplete back-fill, recorded in the measurements document.

findings.title: Both COG buckets have no source-access charge. Their measured metadata differs, while read performance remains unmeasured
findings.text: Both Earth Search collections serve cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs from public buckets in us-west-2 with no authentication and no source-access charge to the reader. Our own compute, storage, and transfer costs are separate and unmeasured. One reader and one windowed read pattern serve both. The older collection needs a version choice where originals sit beside reprocessings, an offset check per item, and most sampled 2022 fallback items lack cloud and snow probability layers. Collection 1 had fewer competing versions in the sample and serves the sampled classification, cloud and snow probability, aerosol, and water-vapour layers as GeoTIFF. The Sinergise JPEG 2000 bucket sits in eu-central-1, its Level-1C bucket is requester pays, its Level-2A pages disagree, and JPEG 2000 reading efficiency depends on file layout and decoder. It stays context. No read time or cost has been measured for any of the three.

findings.title: The two GeoTIFF copies hold the same product in different units, measured on one product, and the older copy's quality layers differ
findings.text: Prototype stage 1 read one 05.11 product, tile 17SKU on 2025-10-15, from both copies and compared six files pixel by pixel. On the three reflectance bands compared, the older copy holds Collection 1's integer minus 1,000, clamped to a minimum of 1, on every one of 99,802,042 pixels valid in both. That is the radiometric offset already applied and reflectance at or below zero discarded. Both catalogs declare the same offset of -0.1 for both copies, so applying the declaration on the older copy would subtract it twice. The scene classification is identical. Aerosol and water vapour are 20 m grids on Collection 1 and 60 m and 10 m grids on the older copy. The older copy's cloud and snow probability assets are JPEG 2000 links into the sentinel-s2-l2a bucket, outside the GeoTIFF benchmark, and whether they open unsigned is untested. Its 10 m bands needed about three times the range requests of Collection 1 for similar bytes. Measurement findings 13 to 15 hold the numbers. One product and three of twelve reflectance bands were checked. The 04.00 items with mixed offset flags remain issue I-05.

issues.title: Cloud dilation flags whole ponds
issues.text: Since baseline 04.00 the scene classification dilates clouds by 80 m, cloud shadows by 40 m, and snow by 20 m. Only clouds with probability above 65 percent and larger than three pixels are dilated. Dilation is suppressed in shoreline regions and at soil and snow boundaries. Over urban areas only clouds above 1000 pixels are dilated. The layer is produced at 20 m, so a qualifying cloud within four cells can flag a 10 m pond. Products before baseline 04.00 are not dilated.
issues.consequence: For small ponds the cloud class can mean a qualifying cloud within 80 m rather than cloud over the pixel. The expectation, unmeasured, is that usable scenes fall faster for small ponds than for lakes. Measure it on the pilot set. How ESA defines shoreline regions is not on the pages read. Semantics change at baseline 04.00 on any archive that mixes original and reprocessed products. The store keeps the class code and the cloud probability so the rule can be revisited.
issues.decision: Owner direction on 2026-09-10: document clearly and revisit later.
issues.plain: Cloud-mask expansion can mark clear pond pixels as cloudy within 80 m of qualifying clouds. Shoreline and other exclusion rules apply.
issues.why: A 10 m pond has no pixel more than 80 m from its edge. Its clear days can vanish from the record while a large lake keeps most of its pixels. The store keeps the raw class and the cloud probability so the rule can change later.

issues.title: Adjacency raises water reflectance from surrounding land
issues.text: Scattered light from nearby land adds to the water signal, most in red and near-infrared. One lake study found chlorophyll retrieval errors higher within 5 km of shore than beyond. That comparison does not isolate a radius for delivered Level-2A reflectance. Effects can extend well beyond a shoreline buffer, with magnitude depending on setting and processing.
issues.consequence: Not a blocker for ingestion. The store serves delivered values plus context: the aerosol optical thickness layer, the pixel's distance to the polygon edge, and the near-land pixel class. The modeling team addresses the correction.
issues.decision: Owner direction on 2026-09-10: document lightly, the modeling team addresses it.
issues.plain: Light scattered from nearby land brightens the water signal, most in red and near-infrared. The effect reaches well beyond the shoreline.
issues.why: Small ponds are all shoreline, so their reflectance carries a land signal the model must account for. Ingestion serves the context the modeling team needs: aerosol, edge distance, and the near-land class.

issues.title: No library default selects pixels for a 10 m pond
issues.text: GDAL rasterization and openEO aggregation select a pixel only when its centre falls inside the polygon. A 10 m pond can select nothing. Coverage-fraction tools report the fraction of each pixel the polygon covers.
issues.consequence: Every water body is stored as three pixel classes computed once per tile and resolution: interior, shoreline, and near-land. A 10 m pond has no interior pixel at any resolution. Consumers see the class and the coverage fraction.
issues.decision: Decision 0002.
issues.plain: Common tools keep a pixel only when its centre falls inside the polygon. A 10 m pond can select no pixel at all.
issues.why: The smallest water bodies in scope would return nothing. Three pixel classes per resolution, with coverage fractions, keep every pond observable and let the model choose its own strictness.

issues.title: Adjacent tiles disagree in their overlap
issues.text: Level-2A is processed per tile. In the overlap between neighbours the classification can differ and the aerosol and surface reflectance are generally different. Some tools fuse overlapping items by first valid pixel or stitch tiles and hide the grid.
issues.consequence: Every record carries the tile it came from and a marker saying whether that tile is the water body's primary tile. Values from two tiles are never averaged. See I-30 for the cross-tile mosaicking investigation the owner requires.
issues.decision: Decision 0002.
issues.plain: Neighbouring tiles are processed separately. Where they overlap, the same ground can get different reflectance and a different class.
issues.why: A pond in an overlap has two values per date. Averaging or silently picking one would hide a real difference. Every record carries its tile, so the model can see and handle both.

issues.title: The radiometric offset arrives in different states
issues.text: From baseline 04.00 the integers carry an offset of minus 1000. Earth Search applied the offset during COG conversion for some items, and each asset's catalog scale and offset describe the remaining conversion. The Sinergise buckets document nothing about the offset. Non-AWS routes pre-apply, harmonize, or clamp. Measured on 2026-09-10 (PR-05): no Collection 1 item carries the provider's offset flag, and every sampled Collection 1 band asset declares a raster:bands offset of -0.1. In the older collection the flag varies per item inside one baseline, true on 3,024 and false on 693 items at 04.00, while every sampled asset from 04.00 declares -0.1 regardless. Measured on 2026-09-14 for one 05.11 product: on three bands and every pixel valid in both, the older copy's integer is Collection 1's minus 1,000, clamped to 1, while both catalogs declare the offset. Finding F-23 and measurement finding 15.
issues.consequence: The store records the conversion state per asset in one representation and reads the values from the asset's own metadata. ESA metadata and catalog metadata use different conventions, mapped in the draft contract. Digital number 0 stays no data. For the 2022 fallback items the two statements cannot both hold, so catalog metadata cannot settle the conversion state.
issues.decision: Draft contract fields scale, offset, and conversion_source. Practice P8. A pixel-level comparison of a GeoTIFF window with its JPEG 2000 alternate, for a flag-true and a flag-false 04.00 item, is a prototyping measurement and a blocker for filling 2022 from the older collection.
issues.plain: Products processed with version 04.00 or later carry an offset. Providers may apply it during conversion, and sampled metadata disagrees about its state.
issues.why: Get it wrong and every reflectance shifts by 0.1, more than most water signals. For 2022 fallback items the metadata contradicts itself, so a pixel check must settle it before any fill.

issues.title: Reader libraries disagree on applying scale and offset
issues.text: rioxarray leaves values unscaled by default. The Zarr opener scales by default. stackstac applies catalog scale and offset by default. odc-stac ignores them.
issues.consequence: One tested conversion function owns the arithmetic. No library default is trusted. A real product per baseline verifies it in prototyping.
issues.decision: Practice P8. Verification is a prototyping measurement.
issues.plain: Popular readers apply, ignore, or partially apply the scale and offset by default, each differently.
issues.why: Two pipelines reading the same file can return different numbers. One tested conversion function owns the arithmetic, and no library default is trusted.

issues.title: One stacking library resamples every band to 10 m by default
issues.text: stackstac upscales all bands to the finest asset resolution with nearest neighbour unless told otherwise. odc-stac returns one requested resolution. rasterio keeps native resolution.
issues.consequence: Bands are stored at native resolution with pixel classes computed per resolution. A lazy-stack workflow needs one stack per resolution.
issues.decision: Practice P3.
issues.plain: One popular stacking library silently resamples every band to 10 m. The 20 m and 60 m bands then look sharper than they are.
issues.why: A resampled pixel can straddle a pond and land. Storing each band at its native resolution, with pixel classes per resolution, keeps the model honest about what each value covers.

issues.title: History spans registration regimes, collections, and undated gaps
issues.text: Refinement of original processing began over Euro-Africa in March 2021 and worldwide in August 2021. Collection 1 reprocessed the archive to 13 December 2023 with refinement, the offset, and dilation, wherever refinement succeeded. Earth Search carries Collection 1 as a separate collection. The gap survey of 2026-09-10 (PR-05, PR-06) measured that collection over 30 tiles: nearly nothing from January to November 2022 in any tile, six months empty everywhere and no month complete anywhere, a global shape, while ESA serves 2022 at baseline 05.10. From December 2022 to December 2023 it holds 05.09 originals where ESA serves 05.10. One Alaska tile is on no Earth Search collection for 52 months, with one Collection 1 item in December 2022 before sustained coverage begins in June 2025. The pre-Collection 1 collection is three months of late 2022. The Copernicus service deleted the originals it reprocessed.
issues.consequence: A 2021 scenario on Collection 1 alone has a hole in 2022 and a baseline change at December 2022 and again at December 2023. The older collection covers 3,842 of the 3,857 missing 2022 acquisitions outside Alaska with 03.01 and 04.00 originals, which differ in offset state, quality layers, and processing from the rest of the history. Distinguish acquisition date from processing baseline in every statement about history. Coverage at a point is smaller than coverage of its tile.
issues.decision: Decision 0003: the 2021 scenario is prototyped first, after this survey. The fallback survey (PR-07) showed the older collection's GeoTIFFs cover the missing 2022 acquisitions outside the absent tile. The fill policy per gap is the owner's next decision. Options are in reviews/2026-09-10-gap-survey.md and the generated report reviews/2026-09-10-gap-survey-report.json. Alaska scope is part of that decision.
issues.plain: The archive is not one uniform series. Products were reprocessed in 2023 and 2024, the route holds them in two collections, and 2022 is nearly missing from the preferred one.
issues.why: A five-year history mixes processing versions and has a hole unless it is filled deliberately. The fill choice decides whether 2022 data carry a different offset state and fewer quality layers than the rest.

issues.title: The refinement flag lives in datastrip metadata
issues.text: The Image_Refining flag is in the Datastrip metadata, not the tile metadata. A route that serves per-tile assets may not expose it.
issues.consequence: The contract field is null where the route does not expose it. Whether either AWS route exposes datastrip metadata is a probe.
issues.decision: Prototyping step.
issues.plain: The flag that says whether a product's geolocation was refined sits in a metadata file the route may not deliver.
issues.why: Without it the store cannot say which dates have the better geolocation. Ponds move by a pixel or more between refined and unrefined dates.

issues.title: Terrain-related displacement depends on viewing geometry
issues.text: DEM-related displacement grows with elevation error and viewing angle. With unchanged elevation error and repeat viewing geometry, that component can cancel between same-orbit images. Other registration errors remain. The 2026-09-11 presentation source checks qualify G10.
issues.consequence: Every record carries the relative orbit. Consumers can compare repeat views while allowing for other alignment errors. The store does not co-register.
issues.decision: Practices P4 and P5.
issues.plain: Terrain-model errors can produce similar position shifts on repeat passes from the same relative orbit. Other alignment errors can remain.
issues.why: Keeping the relative orbit allows consistent-view comparisons. It does not guarantee stable pixel locations across dates.

issues.title: No-data at swath edges is oversampled into fake dark pixels
issues.text: The Level-2A no-data mask is computed at 20 m and oversampled to 10 m, which can fill edge pixels with interpolated low reflectance. ESA recommends filtering with the per-band detector footprint mask. No route's documented quality list names that mask.
issues.consequence: The detector footprint mask is a required layer. Whether either AWS route delivers it is a probe. Without it, swath-edge scenes can look like plausible dark water.
issues.decision: Prototyping step.
issues.plain: At a swath edge the no-data mask is coarser than the bands. Edge pixels can hold interpolated dark values that look like water.
issues.why: A pond at a swath edge can get fake dark readings. The per-band detector footprint mask removes them, and whether the route delivers it is unknown.

issues.title: The scene classification water class is unreliable for ponds
issues.text: The classifier assigns classes spectrally, then cleans water, cloud shadow, and medium-probability cloud pixels against a DEM and a 150 m water map. Its validation excludes water-dominated scenes. Documented failure modes include dark areas classed as cloud shadow.
issues.consequence: Performance over small ponds is unmeasured. The polygon defines the water body. The class code is stored as a hint and never used as the mask.
issues.decision: Practice P13.
issues.plain: The scene classification uses spectral rules and a 150 m reference water map. The cited validation excludes water-dominated scenes.
issues.why: Using the class as the pond mask would drop real ponds and admit shadows. The polygon defines the water body. The class is stored as a hint only.

issues.title: High sun zenith products are under-corrected
issues.text: Products with mean sun zenith above 70 degrees are processed with the angle clipped, and ESA states their reflectance is unfit for quantitative use.
issues.consequence: The store carries the product-level angle as a flag. Winter dates at northern sites are affected.
issues.decision: Draft contract field mean_sun_zenith, practice P11.
issues.plain: When the sun is lower than 20 degrees above the horizon, the processor clips the angle and ESA calls the reflectance unfit for quantitative use.
issues.why: Winter dates at northern sites are affected. The store carries the angle so the model can exclude those dates rather than trust them.

issues.title: Sun glint is not flagged by any delivered layer
issues.text: No Level-2A layer flags glint. ESA documents it as an image feature over water, not a flagged condition.
issues.consequence: A glint index is a candidate derived quality flag under assumption A2. Whether it is detectable from the delivered bands at 10 m ponds is open.
issues.decision: Candidate quality index for prototyping.
issues.plain: Sunlight reflecting off the water surface into the sensor brightens pixels. No delivered layer flags it.
issues.why: Glint looks like turbidity or a bloom. A derived glint flag is a candidate quality index, and whether it can be detected at 10 m ponds is open.

issues.title: Strict inclusion meets registration error
issues.text: Multi-temporal registration is better than 4.5 m at 95 percent, and absolute geolocation about 6 m. Pixel classes are computed once from the polygon, so a pixel classed interior can straddle the shore on some dates.
issues.consequence: The coverage fraction and the shoreline class let a consumer tighten the rule. The near-land buffer keeps the pond in view when it shifts. Revisit once measured on the pilot set.
issues.decision: Revisit after prototyping measurements.
issues.plain: Pixels are classed interior or shoreline once, from the polygon. Between dates the image shifts by several metres, so an interior pixel can straddle the shore on some dates.
issues.why: A strict interior rule is not strict on every date. Coverage fractions and the near-land buffer keep the pond in view when it shifts. Prototyping measures the effect.

issues.title: The primary archive deletes superseded products
issues.text: The Copernicus service removed Collection 0 products up to 13 December 2023. Measured on 2026-09-10 (PR-05): Earth Search's older collection keeps originals beside reprocessed products, with 4,260 mixed-baseline acquisition groups over 30 tiles, and its Collection 1 collection keeps one product per acquisition key except same-day datastrip splits and one mixed-baseline pair, so a date and platform key does not identify one product. Collection 1 also holds 30 acquisitions the Copernicus catalog no longer lists.
issues.consequence: Preserve every ingested revision locally. Both collections can hold multiple products per acquisition, but the survey establishes no retention guarantee for either.
issues.decision: Practice P9. Route retention is a probe.
issues.plain: ESA has removed superseded products. Both AWS copies can hold multiple products per acquisition, with more competing versions in the older copy.
issues.why: A value the model was trained on can disappear at the source. The store keeps every revision it has ingested and never overwrites, so results stay reproducible.

issues.title: Early global Level-2A differs by route
issues.text: Earth Search's older sentinel-2-l2a collection holds June 2017 items over a US box at processing baseline 00.01, a value that matches no ESA baseline. Its Collection 1 and pre-Collection 1 collections hold none for that month. The Sinergise buckets state global Level-2A from January 2017. Whether the 00.01 products were produced by the provider with its own processor is not settled by a page, only suggested by the baseline value.
issues.consequence: For at least mid-2017 in the sampled box, a 2017 scenario on AWS means provider-baseline products. They come from the older collection or the Sinergise buckets, not from ESA Collection 1. Those products predate the offset, dilation, and refinement. Confirm provenance from the provider readme, and probe more months and regions.
issues.decision: Decision 0003 defers the 2017 to 2020 tier until after the 2021 prototype. The provenance probe stays on the list for that later step.
issues.plain: For 2017 the route holds products made by the provider's own processor, with a version number ESA never issued.
issues.why: A 2017-onward history would start with products that lack the offset, dilation, and refinement of later years. The 2017 to 2020 tier is deferred until the 2021 prototype has run.

issues.title: Two pages disagree on whether the Sinergise Level-2A bucket is requester pays
issues.text: The AWS registry lists the Level-2A bucket with an unsigned request example. The provider's readme states the data is in a requester-pays bucket. On 2026-09-10 both buckets answered unsigned HEAD requests with 200, which a requester-pays bucket refuses.
issues.consequence: As sampled, reads from both buckets need no payer header. Cross-region transfer still applies. The readme statement appears stale. Confirm on more prefixes and dates before relying on it.
issues.decision: Earth Search is selected, with COG fallback clarified in decision 0004. JPEG 2000 remains context and a possible source for reference or ancillary checks. Probe PR-04 observed unsigned access on 2026-09-10.
issues.plain: Two provider pages disagree on whether reading the JPEG 2000 bucket costs the reader money. Probes found it answers unsigned requests.
issues.why: The fallback's JPEG 2000 alternates were free to read as sampled. Cross-region transfer still costs. The GeoTIFF fallback avoids the question for most items.

issues.title: JPEG 2000 and cloud-optimized GeoTIFF read differently
issues.text: Earth Search serves cloud-optimized GeoTIFF read by HTTP range requests. The Sinergise buckets serve JPEG 2000, which supports partial decoding by internal tile at higher decode cost. Baseline 05.12, deployed on 4 February 2026, adds tile-part length markers that let decoders reach small regions more efficiently. Earlier products lack them unless reprocessed. The internal tile layout of delivered assets is not documented and is read from the files.
issues.consequence: Bytes, requests, and CPU per pond-scene differ between the two AWS routes and by product baseline. This is the core measurement of the route comparison.
issues.decision: Prototyping benchmark.
issues.plain: Cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs support reads of image blocks around a pond. JPEG 2000 reading efficiency depends on the file and decoder, and needs measurement.
issues.why: Bytes, requests, and compute per pond-scene differ between formats. This is the core cost measurement of the route comparison.

issues.title: Read cost follows blocks touched, not water bodies
issues.text: A windowed read moves the bytes a window touches. GDAL's partial download default is 16 KB and its COG creation default is 512 pixel tiles. A lazy stack defaults to 1024 pixel chunks. A whole product is about 800 MB. These are tool defaults, not properties of the delivered assets.
issues.consequence: Clustered ponds are expected to share reads. The scale driver is expected to be distinct blocks and dates, assumption A17. Request counts, bytes, cache reuse, and decode cost stay unmeasured until the benchmark runs.
issues.decision: Prototyping benchmark on the workload matrix.
issues.plain: A windowed read moves whole internal blocks, not single pixels. Nearby ponds share blocks.
issues.why: Cost scales with distinct blocks and dates, not with the number of ponds. Ten thousand clustered ponds may cost little more than one thousand. The benchmark must test that assumption.

issues.title: No compute platform deduplicates work
issues.text: Lambda, Batch, Kubernetes, Spark, and Dask document retry only. Lambda tells the function to expect duplicate events.
issues.consequence: The draft contract requires immutable revisions and repeat-safe publication. Content-addressed publication keyed by tile, sensing time, baseline, and product is one mechanism. The mechanism is not selected.
issues.decision: Mechanism open. Selected with the workflow.
issues.plain: Every compute platform retries on failure and none promises to run a job exactly once.
issues.why: The same scene can be processed twice. Publication must be repeat-safe, so a second run produces the same record and not a duplicate.

issues.title: Snapshot expiry and logical revision history are different things
issues.text: Iceberg, Icechunk, and S3 Tables document snapshot expiration, and S3 Tables runs maintenance automatically by default. Expiring a snapshot removes time travel to it. Files that surviving snapshots reference are kept. Plain object storage has no atomic update across keys.
issues.consequence: The contract's immutable observation revisions can live as rows with their own availability time, which survive snapshot expiry. Physical snapshot time travel is a separate feature. The retention policy stays open and is decided with the layout.
issues.decision: Decided with the storage layout.
issues.plain: Table formats keep snapshots for time travel and expire them on a schedule. That is not the same as keeping every observation revision.
issues.why: The model needs to reproduce what it saw. Revisions live as rows with their own availability time, which survive snapshot expiry.

issues.title: Small objects and metadata objects carry charges
issues.text: Infrequent-access classes bill at least 128 KB per object with minimum durations. S3 Tables bills monitored objects per month. The Glue catalog bills metadata objects above a free million. Whether a chip or a partition creates such an object depends on the layout and catalog integration.
issues.consequence: Object size, retention, access frequency, and the services actually used are inputs to the layout comparison. No partition rule is selected.
issues.decision: Cost consideration for the layout decision.
issues.plain: Some storage classes bill a minimum object size or retention period. Small files and catalog metadata can add costs.
issues.why: A layout that writes one small object per pond-scene can cost more in overhead than in data. Object size and count are inputs to the layout choice.

issues.title: Publication latency is documented loosely
issues.text: Both AWS routes state availability within a few hours of Copernicus. ESA states Level-2A within 8 hours of sensing.
issues.consequence: No target is set, assumption A11. Latency is a measurement over at least a month of live operation.
issues.decision: Prototyping and later live observation.
issues.plain: Providers say new scenes appear within hours. Nobody states a guarantee.
issues.why: The near-real-time promise to the model has no number behind it yet. Latency is measured over a month of live operation.

issues.title: Revisit density changes across the archive
issues.text: Sentinel-2C replaced 2A in January 2025, and 2A runs an extension campaign since March 2025 over Europe and tropical regions. Adjacent-orbit overlap raises revisit further. Measured on 2026-09-10 (PR-05): reference acquisitions per tile rose with the third satellite, for example 145 in 2021, 148 in 2024, and 175 in 2025 for tile 10SGJ. Two products per acquisition from one pass, split across datastrips, occur for 628 of 21,873 Collection 1 acquisitions.
issues.consequence: Scenes per tile per year are not constant. Benchmarks size on the densest period. Completeness accounting must not assume a fixed cadence.
issues.decision: Input to benchmark design.
issues.plain: Sentinel-2C entered routine operations in 2025. Orbit overlap increases at high latitude, and one pass can produce multiple products for a tile.
issues.why: Scenes per year per pond are not constant. Completeness accounting and benchmark sizing must use the densest period, not an assumed cadence.

issues.title: The two AWS routes may deliver different quality layers
issues.text: Measured on 2026-09-10 (PR-05) from one full item per collection, ingestion software version, and baseline. Collection 1 delivers scene classification, cloud probability, snow probability, aerosol, and water vapour as cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs in a public us-west-2 bucket at every sampled version. The older collection delivers scene classification, aerosol, and water vapour as GeoTIFFs with JPEG 2000 alternates for items ingested by software 0.1.0 and 0.1.1, and adds cloud and snow probability as JPEG 2000 only for items ingested by software 2025.03.06 and later. All but 6 of the 3,717 fallback items at 04.00 for 2022 were ingested by software 0.1.0.
issues.consequence: Quality availability depends on the collection and ingestion version. Most sampled 2022 fallback items lack cloud and snow probability. Fill policy must account for missing layers.
issues.decision: Listing probe done. Whether the store tolerates absent cloud and snow probability for fallback items is part of the fill policy decision.
issues.plain: Sampled Collection 1 items carry cloud and snow probability layers. Most 2022 fallback items lack them, while retaining classification and other layers.
issues.why: Fallback screening may need to rely on classification without probability layers. Conditional cloud dilation and missing layers need testing on the public pilot.

issues.title: Completeness and recovery across the ingestion chain
issues.text: A source observation becomes a catalog item, then an asset-ready product, then a published internal record. Earth Search publishes new items on an SNS topic and daily inventory files. The Sinergise buckets publish SNS topics and inventories. S3 event notifications apply to buckets we own, not to provider buckets. Platforms document retries, not delivery guarantees.
issues.consequence: Track delayed assets, missed or repeated notifications, catalog omissions, and recovery as one issue. Completeness accounting reconciles inventories against published records. The design of that reconciliation is open.
issues.decision: Designed with the workflow.
issues.plain: A scene passes through the provider's catalog, its bucket, our notification, and our store. Any step can lag, drop, or repeat.
issues.why: A missing scene is invisible unless something counts what was expected. Reconciling provider inventories against published records is how the store knows what it lacks.

issues.title: Static pixel classes describe reference geometry, not water on every date
issues.text: Pixel classes are computed once from the polygon. Water extent changes with season and drawdown, shallow bottoms show through clear water, and floating vegetation covers water. The scene classification cannot settle these for small ponds.
issues.consequence: Interior and shoreline labels describe the reference polygon, not verified water presence on a date. Hand this to the modeling team with the glint and adjacency caveats. No change to the extraction geometry.
issues.decision: Interpretation deferred to the modeling team.
issues.plain: Pixel classes come from the polygon. Water shrinks in drought, shallow bottoms show through, and vegetation floats over water.
issues.why: An interior pixel is not guaranteed to be water on every date. The label describes the reference geometry, and the modeling team interprets it with the caveats.

issues.title: Processing baselines keep changing
issues.text: Operational baselines moved from 05.10 in December 2023 to 05.11 in July 2024 and 05.12 in February 2026. ESA has scheduled 05.13 with product specification 15.2 for 21 September 2026. Each baseline can change classification, geometry, masks, or file layout. Measured on 2026-09-10 (PR-05): Collection 1 on Earth Search carries 05.00 for 2021, 05.09 originals from December 2022 to 12 December 2023 where ESA serves 05.10, then 05.10, 05.11 from 23 July 2024, and 05.12 from 4 February 2026. Baselines 99.05 and 99.06 appear on 61 commissioning products of the third satellite in December 2024.
issues.consequence: The store keys every value by baseline and treats a new baseline as a structural change to review, never as a silent continuation. Monitoring must detect a baseline it has not seen. The effects of 05.13 are unassessed. The difference between 05.09 and 05.10 products is unassessed and matters for 2023.
issues.decision: Operational rule for the integration specification. 05.13 effects to assess after deployment.
issues.plain: ESA changes its processing version about once a year. Each change can alter classification, geometry, or file layout.
issues.why: A model trained on one version sees a step change at the next. Every value is keyed by baseline, and a new baseline is treated as a structural change to review.

issues.title: Cross-tile mosaicking is a MAJOR CONCERN
issues.text: Adjacent tiles are processed separately and differ in classification and reflectance in their overlap. Tiles in different UTM zones have different pixel grids. A water body in an overlap or on a zone boundary can have multiple products per date. One near-land buffer can span tiles. Tools that stitch or fuse tiles hide all of this. Measured on 2026-09-10 (PR-05): 7 of 20 survey sites lie in two to four tiles by footprint, so multiple tile products may cover them. Actual usable coverage remains untested.
issues.consequence: MAJOR CONCERN. The owner requires a thorough investigation of cross-tile mosaicking before any stitched value is trusted. The store never mosaics. It keeps every tile's values with a primary marker under the provisional rule of assumption A22. The prototype measures differences between tiles over the same pixels on the same dates, per band and per quality layer. No consumer-facing mosaic is specified before that measurement.
issues.decision: Decision 0003. Owner direction on 2026-09-10: proceed with the provisional primary-tile rule and investigate thoroughly.
issues.plain: A pond near a tile edge may have multiple products per date. Grids or values can differ. Stitching tiles can hide those differences.
issues.why: Seven of twenty survey sites lie in two to four tiles. Which value the model sees, and whether the two agree, is unknown until measured. The store never mosaics, and the difference is measured before any stitched value is trusted.

probes.question: Which Earth Search collections hold Level-2A items for June 2017 over a southeastern US box?
probes.result: No Collection 1 or pre-Collection 1 items. The older sentinel-2-l2a collection holds 24 items at processing baseline 00.01, and the Level-1C collection holds 26 at baseline 02.05.

probes.question: Does the Earth Search Collection 1 collection hold items in the gap periods its README named as of April 2024?
probes.result: June 2019 holds 246 items at baseline 05.00, so that gap is filled for this sample. June 2022 holds none, so that gap persists for this sample.

probes.question: What temporal extent and description do the three Earth Search Level-2A collections declare?
probes.result: All three declare a start of 2015-06-27 and an open end. The pre-Collection 1 collection describes itself as baseline below 05.00 with data and metadata matching Collection 1.

probes.question: Do the Sinergise buckets answer unsigned requests, which requester-pays buckets refuse?
probes.result: Both buckets returned 200 to unsigned HEAD requests on a metadata object and on an imagery object.

probes.question: Which months from 2021-01-01 lack Collection 1 items for the tiles a pilot set touches, what else on the route covers them, and which quality assets does each collection deliver?
probes.result: Scripted survey over 30 tiles from 20 public sites, 900 catalog requests, no imagery. Collection 1 holds no January to November 2022 in any tile, and the gap is global. The older collection covers 3,842 of the 3,857 missing 2022 acquisitions outside Alaska with 03.01 and 04.00 originals. Collection 1 holds 05.09 originals for December 2022 to December 2023 where ESA serves 05.10. One Alaska tile is on no Earth Search collection before June 2025. The offset flag varies per item and contradicts the asset offset for most 04.00 items. Fallback items ingested by early software carry no cloud or snow probability. Numbers and tables are in docs/measurements.md.

probes.question: Is the empty Alaska tile typical of Alaska, and does Hawaii show the same 2022 gap as the contiguous states?
probes.result: Monthly item counts over Alaska, Hawaii, and a northern plains box. Collection 1 falls below 5 percent of its median month in January to November 2022 in all three boxes, except March over Alaska and the plains box. The older collection and Level-1C show no such months. Alaska as a whole holds about 10,000 Collection 1 items per month outside 2022, so the empty tile is specific to its neighbourhood.

probes.question: For every acquisition Collection 1 lacks, does the older collection hold a complete set of cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs in the public bucket, and do those objects exist?
probes.result: Scripted survey over the 405 tile-months the gap survey marked incomplete, 870 requests, headers only on the bucket. Of 5,022 missing acquisitions, 3,840 have an older-collection item with all twelve reflectance bands, the scene classification, aerosol, and water vapour as GeoTIFFs. Five have JPEG 2000 only, all in January 2022. 1,177 have nothing, 1,162 of them in the Alaska tile. The items a fill would use are 03.01 and 04.00 originals with a mixed offset flag and no cloud or snow probability. 702 HEAD requests on 351 sampled items all returned 200 with no request-charged header. Both surveys agree in every tile-month. Numbers are in docs/measurements.md and the generated report.

probes.question: Are the two Earth Search Level-2A collections copies of the same ESA product, and what differs between their items?
probes.result: For tile 17SKU on 2025-10-15 both collections hold the same ESA product, with the same generation time, the same 22 shared assets, the same grid, and the same scale and offset. Collection 1 adds a preview and per-file checksums and sizes. The older collection adds 16 JPEG 2000 links into the Sinergise bucket, a sequence suffix in its id, and a per-item offset flag that contradicts the asset offset. Both collections ingested the acquisition on the same day, so the older one is still growing. Pixels were not compared.
